newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stability pact key to EMU success - Buba's Zeitler.
newsitem.headline: Stability pact key to EMU success - Buba's Zeitler.

text.p: A senior Bundesbank official on Wednesday said a stability pact was essential to the future Euro's success, only one day after a colleague criticised the pact for not going far enough.

Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said on Wednesday that a set of strict rules like those enshrined in the stability pact was a key prerequisite for successful European monetary union.

In an opinion piece published in the German daily Handelsblatt, Zeitler said "A permanently stable Euro not only needs an independent European monetary policy but also demands a willingness (for nations) to give up some sovereignty for national fiscal policies, as envisaged in the stability pact."

But Zeitler's opinion stands at odds with that of Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, who on Tuesday criticised the stability pact for doing too little to keep European nations' budgets in check.

Zeitler, also president of the state central bank in Bavaria, defended the entry criteria for Europe's monetary union, particularly the fixed budget criteria, and argued that the criteria still gave participants enough room to breathe.
Zeitler added that the stability pact's goal was to ensure that this room to breathe would not be transformed into room for countries to create ever larger deficits.
Issing, on the other hand, said the stability pact's biggest shortcoming was its failure to trigger automatic sanctions against countries failing to keep spending in check.
"Unrestrained automaticity would not have been possible but one cannot be satisfied with a decision mechanism in which potential sinners pass judgement on actual sinners," he said.
The stability pact was agreed to by European leaders at the Dublin summit last week and generally hailed as a key building block towards a sound monetary union.

On the Maastricht debt criteria, Zeitler said that the levels set down on the treaty gave sufficient room to stabilise budgetary positions in periods of slow growth while nations should use better years to reduce their deficits.

In order to join the currency union, slated to begin on January 1, 1999, nations must show that their budget deficits do not significantly exceed three percent of gross domestic product and that government debt does not significantly exceed 60 percent of GDP.

Under the terms of the pact, countries which run a budget deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product will face sanctions and fines unless they are forced to overspend by circumstances beyond their control or their economy contracts by two percent or more in a year.
But a country whose economy contracts by just 0.75 percent or more in a year can plead for political clemency to exempt it from the penalties.

Germany had originally sought fully automatic sanctions for countries failing to keep their budgets under control, but was forced in marathon negotiations with nearly all of Europe united against it to give politicians some jurisdiction.
